lead: Dimensional letters give a name or logo physical presence without requiring a full printed background. Their edges, depth and shadows become part of the design, which makes the mounting surface especially important. New York reception walls and business interiors can use this approach for a focused brand statement. Exterior applications need a separate review of the site and mounting requirements. Vision Graphics can help compare the visual direction and organize the details needed to turn approved artwork into a coordinated set of letters.

sections.html: Simple, well-spaced artwork often reads strongly in three dimensions. Thin strokes, small counters and delicate logo elements may need special consideration when moving from screen artwork to physical pieces. Compare the proposed finish against the wall and nearby fixtures before choosing the final look.

Start with the available wall area and the desired relationship to furniture, doors or fascia lines. A placement drawing should establish alignment and spacing. Review mounting methods against the actual substrate; photographs alone cannot confirm what is behind a finished wall.

sections.h2: Compare material, depth and finish together
sections.html: Material and thickness change both the appearance and the way the letters are made and mounted. Review the face and edge colors, the desired shadow and how close visitors will stand. A brushed or polished appearance should be evaluated against the actual wall and lighting. A backer panel may be useful when the logo needs more contrast or when many small elements need to stay together.

Overall size, letter count, logo complexity, material, depth and finish affect fabrication. Mounting height, wall construction, access equipment, removal of an old sign and making good the surface can affect site work. Confirm the mounting method and any property approvals before fabrication. Exterior or illuminated projects require their own scope review; installation is not automatically included with the letters.

Send the original vector logo if available, a straight-on wall photo, a wider room view and approximate available dimensions. Include the project address or ZIP, wall finish, preferred overall size, desired finish and target date. Note whether holes are permitted and whether existing signage needs removal. The approved layout should show letter spacing, placement and the agreed mounting approach.

items.p: Explore solid color or finished acrylic for a defined three-dimensional shape. Review thickness, edge appearance and small artwork details.
Discuss the intended material and finish for the application. Weight, surface appearance and attachment should be considered together.
Compare a metallic surface treatment when the visual effect is the priority. Confirm the underlying material and application suitability.
Group the logo on a panel to establish contrast or simplify the visual composition. Include the panel and its mounting in the overall design.

items: Exterior business identity after site review

items.a_html: Not necessarily. This page focuses on dimensional form; illuminated channel letters require a separate electrical and site review.

items.q: Can you use a detailed logo?
items.a_html: Share the original artwork. Small details may need evaluation for physical production and readability at the intended size.

items.q: Can dimensional letters be installed without drilling?
items.a_html: That depends on the letter construction, weight, surface and installation conditions. Tell us about lease or wall restrictions early. The project team must review the mounting approach; a photograph alone cannot establish a suitable attachment method.

items.q: What makes two similar logo signs cost different amounts?
items.a_html: Material, thickness, letter count, fine details, finish and mounting can differ even when the overall dimensions are similar. Ask for those choices to be identified in the quote, along with any site work, so comparisons reflect the same scope.
